claim: The latent HIV reservoir is a major barrier to HIV cure.
source: The latent HIV reservoir is a major barrier to HIV cure.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Combining latency reversal agents (LRAs) with differing mechanisms of action such as AZD5582, a non-canonical NF-kB activator, and I-BET151, a bromodomain inhibitor is appealing toward inducing HIV-1 reactivation.
source: Combining latency reversal agents (LRAs) with differing mechanisms of action such as AZD5582, a non-canonical NF-kB activator, and I-BET151, a bromodomain inhibitor is appealing toward inducing HIV-1 reactivation.
evidence: This statement reflects the rationale for the study approach based on existing knowledge about LRA combinations.

claim: The AZD5582 & I-BET151 LRA combination is inefficient at activating proviruses in cells of people living with HIV (PLWH).
source: However, even this LRA combination needs improvement as it is inefficient at activating proviruses in cells of people living with HIV (PLWH).
evidence: This is stated as a problem motivating the study, likely based on prior research.

claim: A CRISPR screen in conjunction with AZD5582 & I-BET151 identified Integrator complex subunit 12 (INTS12) as a target to improve this LRA combination.
source: We performed a CRISPR screen in conjunction with AZD5582 & I-BET151 and identified a member of the Integrator complex as a target to improve this LRA combination, specifically Integrator complex subunit 12 (INTS12).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the screen data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Integrator functions as a genome-wide attenuator of transcription that acts on elongation through its RNA cleavage and phosphatase modules.
source: Integrator functions as a genome-wide attenuator of transcription that acts on elongation through its RNA cleavage and phosphatase modules.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the Integrator complex.

claim: Knockout of INTS12 improved latency reactivation at the transcriptional level.
source: Knockout of INTS12 improved latency reactivation at the transcriptional level and is more specific to the HIV-1 provirus than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: INTS12 knockout is more specific to the HIV-1 provirus than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone.
source: Knockout of INTS12 improved latency reactivation at the transcriptional level and is more specific to the HIV-1 provirus than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: INTS12 is present on chromatin at the promoter of HIV.
source: We found that INTS12 is present on chromatin at the promoter of HIV and therefore its effect on HIV may be direct.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of INTS12 on HIV may be direct.
source: We found that INTS12 is present on chromatin at the promoter of HIV and therefore its effect on HIV may be direct.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&Tag data showing INTS12 binding at the HIV promoter.

claim: More RNAPII is present in the gene body of HIV only with the combination of INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: Additionally, we observed more RNAPII in the gene body of HIV only with the combination of INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151, indicating that INTS12 induces a transcriptional elongation block to viral reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data for RPB3 shown in Figure 5B.

claim: INTS12 induces a transcriptional elongation block to viral reactivation.
source: Additionally, we observed more RNAPII in the gene body of HIV only with the combination of INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151, indicating that INTS12 induces a transcriptional elongation block to viral reactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAPII and Ser2p CUT&Tag data in Figure 5.

claim: Knockout of INTS12 increased HIV-1 reactivation in CD4 T cells from virally suppressed PLWH ex vivo.
source: Moreover, knockout of INTS12 increased HIV-1 reactivation in CD4 T cells from virally suppressed PLWH ex vivo, and we detected viral RNA in the supernatant from CD4 T cells of all three virally suppressed PLWH tested upon INTS12 knockout, suggesting that INTS12 prevents full-length HIV RNA production in primary T cells.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Viral RNA was detected in the supernatant from CD4 T cells of all three virally suppressed PLWH tested upon INTS12 knockout.
source: Moreover, knockout of INTS12 increased HIV-1 reactivation in CD4 T cells from virally suppressed PLWH ex vivo, and we detected viral RNA in the supernatant from CD4 T cells of all three virally suppressed PLWH tested upon INTS12 knockout, suggesting that INTS12 prevents full-length HIV RNA production in primary T cells.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from supernatants shown in Figure 6C.

claim: INTS12 prevents full-length HIV RNA production in primary T cells.
source: Moreover, knockout of INTS12 increased HIV-1 reactivation in CD4 T cells from virally suppressed PLWH ex vivo, and we detected viral RNA in the supernatant from CD4 T cells of all three virally suppressed PLWH tested upon INTS12 knockout, suggesting that INTS12 prevents full-length HIV RNA production in primary T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of viral RNA in supernatants upon INTS12 knockout.

claim: INTS12 more generally limits the efficacy of a variety of LRAs with different mechanisms of action.
source: Finally, we found that INTS12 more generally limits the efficacy of a variety of LRAs with different mechanisms of action.
evidence: This is supported by data showing INTS12 KO improves reactivation with TNF-α, anti-CD3/CD28, and SAHA in Figure 7B.

claim: HIV-1 still exists within a latent reservoir in vivo and viral replication returns when antiretroviral therapy (ART) is interrupted.
source: Despite advancements in keeping viral loads below detectable limits, HIV-1 still exists within a latent reservoir in vivo and viral replication returns when antiretroviral therapy (ART) is interrupted (Davey et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davey et al., 1999.

claim: HIV-1 predominately infects memory CD4+ T cells.
source: HIV-1 predominately infects memory CD4+ T cells (reviewed in Ait-Ammar et al., 2019; Cohn et al., 2020), and while many acutely infected cells, particularly the more differentiated effector memory cells, die off rapidly upon infection due to cytopathic effects, some cells can revert to a resting state where the provirus becomes transcriptionally silent (reviewed in Duggan et al., 2023; Mbonye and Karn, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Many acutely infected cells, particularly the more differentiated effector memory cells, die off rapidly upon infection due to cytopathic effects.
source: HIV-1 predominately infects memory CD4+ T cells (reviewed in Ait-Ammar et al., 2019; Cohn et al., 2020), and while many acutely infected cells, particularly the more differentiated effector memory cells, die off rapidly upon infection due to cytopathic effects, some cells can revert to a resting state where the provirus becomes transcriptionally silent (reviewed in Duggan et al., 2023; Mbonye and Karn, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Some infected cells can revert to a resting state where the provirus becomes transcriptionally silent.
source: HIV-1 predominately infects memory CD4+ T cells (reviewed in Ait-Ammar et al., 2019; Cohn et al., 2020), and while many acutely infected cells, particularly the more differentiated effector memory cells, die off rapidly upon infection due to cytopathic effects, some cells can revert to a resting state where the provirus becomes transcriptionally silent (reviewed in Duggan et al., 2023; Mbonye and Karn, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The reservoir of latently infected cells is largely invisible to the immune system and not sensitive to enhanced ART.
source: These infected resting memory cells form the HIV reservoir that is largely invisible to the immune system and not sensitive to enhanced ART (Siliciano and Siliciano, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siliciano and Siliciano, 2024.

claim: The reservoir of latently infected cells decays slowly and is maintained by both external stimuli and homeostatic proliferation even after initiation of ART.
source: The reservoir of latently infected cells decays slowly and is maintained by both external stimuli and homeostatic proliferation even after initiation of ART (reviewed in Cohn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The major barrier to HIV cure is the existence of an ART-insensitive and long-lived latent reservoir that is largely not sensed by the immune system.
source: Thus, the major barrier to HIV cure is the existence of this ART-insensitive and long-lived latent reservoir that is largely not sensed by the immune system (Chun and Fauci, 1999), reviewed in Duggan et al., 2023; Mbonye and Karn, 2024.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research and review articles.

claim: The 'shock-and-kill' strategy uses small-molecule compounds called latency reversal agents (LRAs) to transcriptionally activate latent cells, so that immune-mediated mechanisms can then recognize and kill infected cells.
source: One strategy being explored to target the latent reservoir, called 'shock-and-kill', uses small-molecule compounds called latency reversal agents (LRAs) to transcriptionally activate latent cells, so that immune-mediated mechanisms can then recognize and kill infected cells (Archin et al., 2012), reviewed in Maina et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research and review articles.

claim: Inducing HIV-1 activation from latency is challenging because the latent reservoir size varies between people and heterogeneous HIV integration sites can influence the reactivation of infected cells.
source: However, inducing HIV-1 activation from latency is challenging because the latent reservoir size varies between people and heterogeneous HIV integration sites can influence the reactivation of infected cells (reviewed in Ait-Ammar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Activation of latently infected resting T cells has not yet been able to induce HIV-1 replication from more than a fraction of the cells with a replication-competent provirus.
source: Moreover, activation of latently infected resting T cells has not yet been able to induce HIV-1 replication from more than a fraction of the cells with a replication-competent provirus (Ho et al., 2013; Siliciano and Siliciano, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research articles.

claim: Transcriptional repression of HIV-1 in its latent state is multifactorial, and it is known to be affected by repressive chromatin modifications and blocks to both transcription initiation and transcription elongation.
source: Transcriptional repression of HIV-1 in its latent state is multifactorial, and it is known to be affected by repressive chromatin modifications and blocks to both transcription initiation and transcription elongation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HIV latency mechanisms.

claim: Several classes of LRAs have been identified that can undo one or more blocks to latency reversal.
source: Several classes of LRAs have been identified that can undo one or more blocks to latency reversal (Stoszko et al., 2019), reviewed in Rodari et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research and review articles.

claim: AZD5582 is an LRA that targets a transcription initiation block by activating the noncanonical NF-kB pathway.
source: For example, AZD5582 is an LRA that targets a transcription initiation block by activating the noncanonical NF-kB pathway (Hennessy et al., 2013; Pache et al., 2020) and has been shown to induce HIV transcription in HIV latency cell line models as well as induce viremia in animal models (Nixon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research articles.

claim: AZD5582 has been shown to induce HIV transcription in HIV latency cell line models as well as induce viremia in animal models.
source: For example, AZD5582 is an LRA that targets a transcription initiation block by activating the noncanonical NF-kB pathway (Hennessy et al., 2013; Pache et al., 2020) and has been shown to induce HIV transcription in HIV latency cell line models as well as induce viremia in animal models (Nixon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nixon et al., 2020.

claim: BET inhibitors undo a block to transcription elongation by targeting various bromodomain-containing proteins.
source: Another class of LRAs are BET inhibitors that undo a block to transcription elongation by targeting various bromodomain-containing proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BET inhibitors.

claim: I-BET151 is thought to reverse HIV latency by either blocking host Brd4 from binding to P-TEFb to facilitate P-TEFb availability for HIV Tat or more generally by increasing the amount of P-TEFb not bound to the 7SK complex.
source: I-BET151 is a pan-BET inhibitor that is thought to reverse HIV latency by either blocking host Brd4 from binding to P-TEFb to facilitate P-TEFb availability for HIV Tat (Jang et al., 2005; Schröder et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2005) or more generally by increasing the amount of P-TEFb not bound to the 7SK complex (Turner et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research articles.

claim: No single LRA has been potent enough to reactivate the majority of the latent proviruses nor specific enough to HIV to not cause cytotoxicity.
source: Currently, no single LRA has been potent enough to reactivate the majority of the latent proviruses nor specific enough to HIV to not cause cyotoxicity (reviewed in Debrabander et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Combinations of LRAs with different mechanisms of action have shown synergy in HIV latency reversal in different model systems including the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: On the other hand, combinations of LRAs with different mechanisms of action have shown synergy in HIV latency reversal in different model systems including the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Dai et al., 2022; Falcinelli et al., 2022; Laird et al., 2015) reviewed in Rodari et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research and review articles.

claim: The combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 is synergistic in activation of HIV in latency cell line models.
source: However, while the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 is synergistic in activation of HIV in latency cell line models, and can induce robust HIV transcription initiation ex vivo in primary CD4+ T cells from virally suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH), it failed to induce full-length proviral transcription in the ex vivo system (Falcinelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falcinelli et al., 2022.

claim: The combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 can induce robust HIV transcription initiation ex vivo in primary CD4+ T cells from virally suppressed PLWH.
source: However, while the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 is synergistic in activation of HIV in latency cell line models, and can induce robust HIV transcription initiation ex vivo in primary CD4+ T cells from virally suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH), it failed to induce full-length proviral transcription in the ex vivo system (Falcinelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falcinelli et al., 2022.

claim: The combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 failed to induce full-length proviral transcription in the ex vivo system.
source: However, while the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 is synergistic in activation of HIV in latency cell line models, and can induce robust HIV transcription initiation ex vivo in primary CD4+ T cells from virally suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH), it failed to induce full-length proviral transcription in the ex vivo system (Falcinelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falcinelli et al., 2022.

claim: There exist additional blocks to HIV reactivation that even potent LRA combinations currently cannot overcome.
source: Thus, there exist additional blocks to HIV reactivation that even potent LRA combinations currently cannot overcome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AZD5582 & I-BET151 fails to induce full-length transcription.

claim: Knockout of ING3, a member of the NuA4 histone acetylation complex, could improve the potency and the specificity of AZD5582, both in J-Lat model systems and in a primary T cell model of latency.
source: Specifically, knockout of ING3, a member of the NuA4 histone acetylation complex, could improve the potency and the specificity of AZD5582, both in J-Lat model systems and in a primary T cell model of latency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors' lab.

claim: INTS12 is a subunit of the Integrator complex that is thought to act as a reader to link the complex to chromatin.
source: INTS12 is a subunit of the Integrator complex that is thought to act as a reader to link the complex to chromatin (Welsh and Gardini, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Welsh and Gardini, 2023.

claim: The Integrator complex functions as a genome-wide attenuator of mRNA transcription where it can antagonize transcription with both its cleavage and phosphatase modules.
source: The Integrator complex functions as a genome-wide attenuator of mRNA transcription where it can antagonize transcription with both its cleavage and phosphatase modules (Hu et al., 2023), and members of Integrator have been shown to modulate transcription at the HIV LTR previously (Lykke-Andersen et al., 2021; Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2023.

claim: Members of Integrator have been shown to modulate transcription at the HIV LTR previously.
source: The Integrator complex functions as a genome-wide attenuator of mRNA transcription where it can antagonize transcription with both its cleavage and phosphatase modules (Hu et al., 2023), and members of Integrator have been shown to modulate transcription at the HIV LTR previously (Lykke-Andersen et al., 2021; Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lykke-Andersen et al., 2021 and Stadelmayer et al., 2014.

claim: Knocking out INTS12 reactivates HIV on its own and improves reactivation with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment.
source: We found that knocking out INTS12 reactivates HIV on its own and improves reactivation with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The combination of INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 increases the potency of reactivation.
source: RNA-seq analysis showed that INTS12 knockout (KO) more specifically reactivates HIV compared to AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone, and the combination of INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 increases the potency of reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: There is an increase in bound elongation-competent RNAPII in the gene body of HIV with INTS12 KO paired with AZD5582 & I-BET151 that is not seen with either KO or LRA treatment alone.
source: Additionally, we have evidence of an elongation block being overcome with INTS12 KO paired with AZD5582 & I-BET151 specifically showing an increase in bound elongation-competent RNAPII in the gene body of HIV that is not seen with either KO or LRA treatment alone.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data in Figure 5.

claim: INTS12 is bound to the viral promoter and therefore may be acting directly on viral transcription.
source: We found that INTS12 is bound to the viral promoter and therefore may be acting directly on viral transcription.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data in Figure 5A and inferred from the binding data.

claim: The cleavage module, phosphatase module, and core of the Integrator complex are all involved in the control of HIV-1 latency in addition to the reader, INTS12.
source: Furthermore, we used the HIV-CRISPR screen approach to probe the Integrator complex as a whole and predict Integrator members comprising the cleavage module, phosphatase module, and core to all be involved in the control of HIV-1 latency in addition to the reader, INTS12.
evidence: This is supported by Screen #2 data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockout of INTS12 can increase reactivation with diverse classes of LRAs.
source: Lastly, we show that knockout of INTS12 can increase reactivation with diverse classes of LRAs, suggesting that INTS12 is a general block to HIV reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B showing increased reactivation with TNF-α, anti-CD3/CD28, and SAHA.

claim: INTS12 is a general block to HIV reactivation.
source: Lastly, we show that knockout of INTS12 can increase reactivation with diverse classes of LRAs, suggesting that INTS12 is a general block to HIV reactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that INTS12 KO improves multiple different LRAs.

claim: The HuEpi library contains 5309 sgRNAs total (839 genes with six guides/gene) that comprises histone binders/modifiers and other general chromatin-associated proteins.
source: We used a custom human epigenome guide library (HuEpi library) that contains 5309 sgRNAs total (839 genes with six guides/gene) that comprises histone binders/modifiers and other general chromatin-associated proteins, which casts a wide net on general epigenetic factors (further description of this library and the major gene ontology categories targeted has been published; Hsieh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a description of the methods and materials used in the study.

claim: The HuEpi library was validated as containing guides to multiple genes involved in HIV-1 latency.
source: We previously validated the HuEpi library as containing guides to multiple genes involved in HIV-1 latency (Hsieh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: J-Lat 10.6 and J-Lat 5A8 are clonal Jurkat T-lymphocyte cell lines that contain latent HIV.
source: Here, we conducted additional screens in two cell lines, J-Lat 10.6 and J-Lat 5A8, that are clonal Jurkat T-lymphocyte cell lines that contain latent HIV.
evidence: This is a description of the cell lines used in the study.

claim: J-Lat 10.6 and J-Lat 5A8 differ in integration site and HIV drug reactivation profiles.
source: We chose these cells because they differ in integration site and HIV drug reactivation profiles (Chan et al., 2013; Jordan et al., 2003; Spina et al., 2013; Telwatte et al., 2019) and wanted to identify commonly enriched genes that were not integration site specific.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research articles.

claim: Gene hits KAT5, CUL3, ACTL6A, TAF5, DNMT1, DMAP1, VPS72, YEATS4, SRCAP, and ING3 have been validated previously using the same HuEpi library.
source: With this approach, we identified gene hits that have been validated previously using the same HuEpi library (Hsieh et al., 2023): KAT5, CUL3, ACTL6A, TAF5, DNMT1, DMAP1, VPS72, YEATS4, SRCAP, and ING3 (Figure 1B and C, full screen list and results in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Knockout of ING3 was previously shown to improve AZD5582 treatment for activation of latent HIV-1.
source: Knockout of ING3 was previously shown to improve AZD5582 treatment for activation of latent HIV-1 (Hsieh et al., 2023), and also shows up as a candidate hit in the present screen done the presence of both AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: INTS12 was seen in a previous study but was not followed up on in that study.
source: Our top hit, INTS12, here was also seen in our previous study (Hsieh et al., 2023), but was not followed up on in that study.
evidence: This is stated as context for the current study.

claim: Gene hits INTS12, TRRAP, RNF20, BRD2, TAF3, TAF4, UBE2D3, and UBE2H are predicted to improve the AZD5582 & I-BET151 combination specifically in both J-Lat lines tested.
source: Gene hits of interest that we identified that are predicted to improve the AZD5582 & I-BET151 combination specifically in both J-Lat lines tested including (shown in blue or purple, Figure 1B and C): INTS12, TRRAP, RNF20, BRD2, TAF3, TAF4, UBE2D3, and UBE2H.
evidence: This is supported by screen data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: EZH2 and PPP2CA were only predicted to improve AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment in one cell line.
source: Some hits, EZH2 and PPP2CA, were only predicted to improve AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment in one cell line.
evidence: This is stated based on the screen results.

claim: The screen predicted that inhibition of EZH2 would increase the potency of AZD5582 & I-BET151 to activate HIV-1 from latency in J-Lat 5A8 cells.
source: That is, the screen predicted that inhibition of EZH2 would increase the potency of AZD5582 & I-BET151 to activate HIV-1 from latency in J-Lat 5A8 cells.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the screen data.

claim: Tazemetostat increases reactivation of HIV-1 in the presence of AZD5582 & I-BET151 to much higher levels than AZD5582 & I-BET151 alone or Tazemetostat alone.
source: Indeed, we found that Tazemetostat increases reactivation of HIV-1 in the presence of AZD5582 & I-BET151 to much higher levels than AZD5582 & I-BET151 alone or Tazemetostat alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Integrator complex is known to play a role in the negative regulation of elongating transcripts.
source: The Integrator complex is known to play a role in the negative regulation of elongating transcripts (Elrod et al., 2019; Tatomer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research articles.

claim: Previous studies have shown that some Integrator members are recruited to the HIV LTR and regulate HIV transcript length.
source: Moreover, previous studies have shown that some Integrator members are recruited to the HIV LTR and regulate HIV transcript length (Stadelmayer et al., 2014), although INTS12 had not been previously implicated in HIV regulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stadelmayer et al., 2014.

claim: INTS12 had not been previously implicated in HIV regulation.
source: Moreover, previous studies have shown that some Integrator members are recruited to the HIV LTR and regulate HIV transcript length (Stadelmayer et al., 2014), although INTS12 had not been previously implicated in HIV regulation.
evidence: This is stated as context for the novelty of the current findings.

claim: In AAVS1 knockout cells, there is minimal reactivation in the DMSO control, a small amount of HIV induction from AZD5582 or I-BET151 alone, and synergy with AZD5582 & I-BET151 used in combination.
source: As expected, we find in AAVS1 knockout cells that there is minimal reactivation in the DMSO control, a small amount of HIV induction from AZD5582 or I-BET151 alone, and we observe synergy with AZD5582 & I-BET151 used in combination (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Knocking out INTS12 alone in the absence of added LRAs shows a modest increase in the amount of virus detected in the supernatant.
source: Knocking out INTS12 alone in the absence of added LRAs also shows a modest increase in the amount of virus detected in the supernatant (Figure 2A and B, DMSO), indicating that INTS12 itself is imposing a block to reactivation that is relieved upon knockout.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: INTS12 itself is imposing a block to reactivation that is relieved upon knockout.
source: Knocking out INTS12 alone in the absence of added LRAs also shows a modest increase in the amount of virus detected in the supernatant (Figure 2A and B, DMSO), indicating that INTS12 itself is imposing a block to reactivation that is relieved upon knockout.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that INTS12 KO alone increases virus release.

claim: In the presence of drug treatments, INTS12 knockout improves reactivation of either AZD5582 or I-BET151 alone.
source: In the presence of drug treatments, INTS12 knockout improves reactivation of either AZD5582 or I-BET151 alone, and we see the most HIV reactivation when INTS12 knockout is treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 in combination (Figure 2A and B), as the screen predicted (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The most HIV reactivation is seen when INTS12 knockout is treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 in combination.
source: In the presence of drug treatments, INTS12 knockout improves reactivation of either AZD5582 or I-BET151 alone, and we see the most HIV reactivation when INTS12 knockout is treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 in combination (Figure 2A and B), as the screen predicted (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Flow cytometry data showed a greater percentage of cells are activated from INTS12 KO alone and in combination with AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: Flow cytometry data using the expression of GFP in the provirus gave similar results and showed a greater percentage of cells are activated from INTS12 KO alone and in combination with AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: No differences in cell growth were observed between AAVS1 KO and INTS12 KO cells over time.
source: To ensure cell viability did not contribute to this phenotype, we measured cell proliferation in our AAVS1 KO and INTS12 KO cells over time and observed no differences in cell growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reactivation of the HIV-1 provirus in the INTS12 KO cells that were complemented with an INTS12 expression vector were equivalent to the control AAVS1 KO cells with the same INTS12 expression vector.
source: We found that reactivation of the HIV-1 provirus in the INTS12 KO cells that were complemented with an INTS12 expression vector were now equivalent to the control AAVS1 KO cells with the same INTS12 expression vector (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: INTS12 is responsible for a negative effect on HIV expression in the presence of LRAs, AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: These results show that INTS12 is responsible for a negative effect on HIV expression in the presence of LRAs, AZD5582 & I-BET151.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation experiment showing that restoring INTS12 reverses the reactivation phenotype.

claim: The RNA-seq trend matches what was seen with the virus release assay where the INTS12 KO alone reactivates HIV, and INTS12 KO further improves reactivation with AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: We observed that the RNA-seq trend matches what we saw with the virus release assay (Figure 2B) where the INTS12 KO alone reactivates HIV, and INTS12 KO further improves reactivation with AZD5582 & I-BET151.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A compared to virus release data in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar pileup trends along the length of the provirus are observed for different conditions.
source: Reads were also mapped along the length of the HIV provirus (Figure 3B) using PMA and ionomycin (PMAi) -treated cells in this comparison as a positive control known to induce full-length transcripts (Falcinelli et al., 2022; Figure 3B, bottom row). We observe the same differences quantified in (Figure 3A) as well as similar pileup trends along the length of the provirus.
evidence: This is supported by pileup data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PMA and ionomycin-treated cells are a positive control known to induce full-length transcripts.
source: Reads were also mapped along the length of the HIV provirus (Figure 3B) using PMA and ionomycin (PMAi) -treated cells in this comparison as a positive control known to induce full-length transcripts (Falcinelli et al., 2022; Figure 3B, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falcinelli et al., 2022.

claim: It is likely the total RNA-seq is only looking at full-length RNA detection because RNAs lacking a polyA tail are degraded rapidly.
source: Because RNAs lacking a polyA tail are degraded rapidly (Biziaev et al., 2024), it is unclear whether those RNAs were successfully captured in our assay, and it is likely we are only looking at full-length RNA detection.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge about RNA stability and the RNA-seq method used.

claim: The total RNA-seq results show that INTS12 KO increases HIV proviral activation at the transcriptional level.
source: Nevertheless, the total RNA-seq results show that INTS12 KO increases HIV proviral activation at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment results in 80 genes upregulated and 306 genes downregulated compared to DMSO-treated AAVS1 KO cells.
source: We first compared our AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment condition to the DMSO-treated AAVS1 KO cells and found that 80 genes were upregulated and 306 were downregulated, and that HIV was the most upregulated transcript with the highest fold-change (FC) and was highly expressed as indicated by counts per million (CPM) (Figure 4A, left panel), similar to previous work (Falcinelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression data shown in Figure 4A, left panel.

claim: HIV was the most upregulated transcript with the highest fold-change and was highly expressed with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment.
source: We first compared our AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment condition to the DMSO-treated AAVS1 KO cells and found that 80 genes were upregulated and 306 were downregulated, and that HIV was the most upregulated transcript with the highest fold-change (FC) and was highly expressed as indicated by counts per million (CPM) (Figure 4A, left panel), similar to previous work (Falcinelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression data shown in Figure 4A, left panel.

claim: INTS12 KO alone is even more specific to HIV transcripts than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment, with only 70 upregulated genes and only 3 downregulated genes.
source: Surprisingly, given the more widespread reported role of Integrator in transcription, we find that INTS12 KO alone is even more specific to HIV transcripts than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment, where we find the same level of enrichment of HIV as the previous comparison with an FC of 8, but there are only 70 upregulated genes and only 3 downregulated genes (Figure 4A, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression data shown in Figure 4A, middle panel.

claim: INTS12 is more important to HIV transcription than it is to any other transcriptional unit in J-Lat cells.
source: This indicates that INTS12 is more important to HIV transcription than it is to any other transcriptional unit in J-Lat cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that INTS12 KO specifically affects HIV with minimal effects on other genes.

claim: The combination of INTS12 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 showed an even greater enrichment of the HIV transcripts at a fold change of approximately 28.
source: Furthermore, the transcriptional landscape of the combination of INTS12 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 compared to AAVS1 KO cells that were treated with DMSO (Figure 4A, right panel) showed an even greater enrichment of the HIV transcripts at a FC of ~28 (Log2(fold change) = 4.8).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression data shown in Figure 4A, right panel.

claim: The gain of potency from INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 came with some loss of specificity as there was greater dysregulation of the host with 255 upregulated genes and 159 downregulated genes.
source: However, this gain of potency came with some loss of specificity as there was greater dysregulation of the host with 255 upregulated genes and 159 downregulated genes compared to the INTS12 knockout alone or the AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone.

claim: Among the host genes most prominently affected by INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151 are MAFA, MAFB, and ID2.
source: Among the host genes most prominently affected by INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151 are MAFA, MAFB, and ID2 (full list of genes and results in Supplementary file 3, tabs 1–4).
evidence: This is stated based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151 was much more specific to HIV-1 than PMAi, which affects thousands of host transcripts.
source: Nonetheless, INTS12 knockout with AZD5582 & I-BET151 was much more specific to HIV-1 than PMAi, which can robustly activate HIV but at the cost of affecting thousands of host transcripts (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression data comparing conditions in Figure 4.

claim: INTS12 knockout acts at the transcriptional level in activating HIV from latency.
source: Thus, we find that INTS12 knockout acts at the transcriptional level in activating HIV from latency and is more specific for the HIV LTR than AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment alone.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased HIV transcripts.

claim: INTS12 knockout indeed improves potency of reactivation of AZD5582 & I-BET151 but at the cost of some specificity.
source: We also find that INTS12 knockout indeed improves potency of reactivation of AZD5582 & I-BET151 but at the cost of some specificity.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased HIV transcripts but also more host gene dysregulation.

claim: INTS12 is present at the LTR of HIV-1 as the signal over the LTR is greater in the AAVS1 KO cells than in cells with the partial INTS12 knockout.
source: Using this approach, we observed that INTS12 is indeed at the LTR of HIV-1 as the signal over the LTR is greater in the AAVS1 KO cells than in cells with the partial INTS12 knockout (Figure 5A, left panel, compare top two rows with bottom two rows).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: INTS12 localization extends past the LTR, matching what has been seen previously, where Integrator members localize to sites of pausing which are past the site of initiation.
source: We also saw this effect with a different INTS12 antibody (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We found that that INTS12 localization extends past the LTR, matching what has been seen previously, where Integrator members localize to sites of pausing which are past the site of initiation (Elrod et al., 2019; Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data and citations to previous studies.

claim: INTS12 binds to the HIV promoter, suggesting that INTS12 represses HIV-1 activation from latency through a direct mechanism.
source: These results indicate INTS12 binds to the HIV promoter, suggesting that INTS12 represses HIV-1 activation from latency through a direct mechanism.

claim: Similar levels of RPB3 are seen in region 1 for all four conditions.
source: We see similar levels of RPB3 in region 1 for all four conditions.

claim: There was a dramatic statistically significant increase in RPB3/RNAPII occupancy in the body of the provirus (region 2) only with both INTS12 KO and AZD5582 & I-BET151 together.
source: We found that there was a dramatic statistically significant increase in RPB3/RNAPII occupancy in the body of the provirus (region 2) only with both INTS12 KO and AZD5582 & I-BET151 together (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No increase in RNAPII was seen in the gene downstream of the integrated provirus (region 3).
source: We did not see this increase in RNAPII when we examined the gene downstream of the integrated provirus (region 3).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Evidence of elongation-competent RNAPII was observed for AAVS1 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 and INTS12 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151.
source: We observed evidence of elongation-competent RNAPII for two conditions with LRAs: AAVS1 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 and our INTS12 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Figure 5C), as we saw a significant increase in reads in region 2 compared to the AAVS1 KO treated with DMSO control.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data for Ser2p shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No statistically significant differences in RNAPII Ser5 phosphorylation were observed in any region for the conditions tested.
source: When we tested RNAPII Ser5 phosphorylation, a marker not associated with elongation, we did not observe any statistically significant differences in any region for the same conditions tested in Figure 5B and C (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data for Ser5p shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The data support the hypothesis that the combination of INTS12 with AZD5582 & I-BET151 specifically overcomes an elongation block that the INTS12 KO and AZD5582 & I-BET151 alone cannot overcome.
source: Therefore, these data support the hypothesis that the combination of INTS12 with AZD5582 & I-BET151 specifically overcomes an elongation block that the INTS12 KO and AZD5582 & I-BET151 alone cannot overcome.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&Tag data showing increased elongation-competent RNAPII only with the combination.

claim: INTS12 KO trends upward for viral RNA expression in all six donors and this increase is statistically significant in four donors when treated with DMSO.
source: In Figure 6A, when we treat donors with the vehicle control (DMSO), we find that INTS12 KO trends upward for viral RNA expression in all six donors and this increase is statistically significant in four donors (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LRAs alone could activate viral RNA expression in primary cells from PLWH.
source: These same samples were treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Figure 6B), and we found that although LRAs alone could activate viral RNA expression (compare samples in Figure 6A with Figure 6B), the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 paired with the INTS12 KO shows an even further increase in HIV-1 reactivation that was statistically significant in four out of six donors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 paired with the INTS12 KO shows an even further increase in HIV-1 reactivation that was statistically significant in four out of six donors.
source: These same samples were treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 (Figure 6B), and we found that although LRAs alone could activate viral RNA expression (compare samples in Figure 6A with Figure 6B), the combination of AZD5582 & I-BET151 paired with the INTS12 KO shows an even further increase in HIV-1 reactivation that was statistically significant in four out of six donors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For donor PH543, there is an increase from the INTS12 KO itself and robust activation from AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment itself; however, there was no further increase from INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment.
source: For donor PH543 (upside-down triangle), we found that there is an increase from the INTS12 KO itself (Figure 6A, right panel), and robust activation from AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment itself (Figure 6B, right panel); however, there was no further increase from INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from primary cells shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Degree of reactivation was correlated with reservoir size as donors PH504 and PH543 have the largest HIV reservoirs.
source: Degree of reactivation was correlated with reservoir size as donors PH504 (star symbol) and PH543 (upside-down triangle) have the largest HIV reservoirs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the primary cell data and reservoir measurements.

claim: The screen was able to identify INTS12 as a barrier to HIV-1 reactivation in PLWH as there is reactivation from INTS12 knockout alone and improvement of AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment with the addition of INTS12 knockout in a majority of virally suppressed PLWH tested ex vivo.
source: This data shows that our screen was able to identify INTS12 as a barrier to HIV-1 reactivation in PLWH as we find that there is reactivation from INTS12 knockout alone and improvement of AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment with the addition of INTS12 knockout in a majority of virally suppressed PLWH tested ex vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the primary cell data in Figure 6.

claim: For all three donors, INTS12 KO was able to improve reactivation either on its own or in the presence of AZD5582 & I-BET151 when measuring viral RNA in the supernatant.
source: Importantly, we observed for all three donors that INTS12 KO was able to improve reactivation either on its own or in the presence of AZD5582 & I-BET151.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from supernatants shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Donor 543 showed a robust increase from the pairing of INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment when measuring gag RNA in the supernatant.

evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from supernatants shown in Figure 6C.

source: The differences between Figure 6C and B for donor 543 could be due to the timing of the assay, or alternatively, pairing INTS12 KO with AZD5582 & I-BET151 results in more efficient full-length viral RNA such that we do not see an increase within the cell with the addition of INTS12 KO (Figure 6B) because there is an increased amount of RNA into the supernatant (Figure 6C, difference between LRA with or without INTS12 KO).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: The majority of donors are responsive to INTS12 KO with or without AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment and this reactivation leads to full-length HIV that can be detected in the supernatant.
source: Nevertheless, we can conclude that the majority of these donors are responsive to INTS12 KO with or without AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment and that this reactivation leads to full-length HIV that can be detected in the supernatant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the primary cell data in Figure 6.

claim: Integrator members are important for HIV latency.
source: Previous studies have shown that Integrator members are important for HIV latency (Stadelmayer et al., 2014), and some have done so in the context of combination LRA treatment (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only INTS12 was included in the CRISPR guide library of the 15-member Integrator complex in the initial screen of epigenetic factors.
source: In our initial screen of epigenetic factors (Figure 1), only INTS12 was included in the CRISPR guide library of the 15-member Integrator complex.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the initial screen.

claim: A library of guides was made that included all Integrator members (with the exception of INTS15 that was not known at the time of library construction).
source: In order to more comprehensively interrogate the role of Integrator complex members in HIV latency, we remade a library of guides in the HIV-CRISPR vector where we included all Integrator members (with the exception of INTS15 that was not known at the time of library construction Offley et al., 2023; Replogle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the methods for Screen #2.

claim: INTS12 is again predicted to improve the AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment in Screen #2 as it falls above the average NTCs.
source: We took this new library (herein, Screen #2) and treated J-Lat 10.6 cells with 1 nM AZD5582 & 2.5 µM I-BET151 for 24 hr (Figure 7) and found INTS12 is again predicted to improve the AZD5582 & I-BET151 treatment as it falls above the average NTCs.
evidence: This is supported by Screen #2 data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All members of the cleavage module (INTS11, INTS9, INTS4), all members of the phosphatase module (INTS5, INTS6, INTS8), and all members of the core (INTS1, INTS2, INTS7) score positively in Screen #2.
source: Importantly, however, all members of the cleavage module: INTS11, INTS9, INTS4; all members of the phosphatase module: INTS5, INTS6, INTS8; and all members of the core: INTS1, INTS2, INTS7 score positively in our screen.
evidence: This is supported by Screen #2 data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A large majority of the Integrator complex, consisting of the cleavage module, phosphatase module, core, and INTS12, but not the SOSS complex or the enhancer/arm module, likely play a role in HIV latency reversal in the presence of LRAs.
source: Thus, we predict that a large majority of the Integrator complex, consisting of the cleavage module, phosphatase module, core, and INTS12, but not the SOSS complex or the enhancer/arm module, likely play a role in HIV latency reversal in the presence of LRAs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on Screen #2 data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: INTS12 KO is able to increase reactivation with TNF-α and anti-CD3/anti-CD28 co-stimulation.
source: We took our AAVS1 KO cells or INTS12 KO cells and reactivated with TNF-α, a canonical NF-kB activator, or anti-CD3/anti-CD28 co-stimulation that activates T cells through the T cell receptor and observed that INTS12 KO is able to increase reactivation with both of these stimuli (Figure 7B, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by RT assay data shown in Figure 7B, left panel.

claim: Greater reactivation is observed in 250 nM and 1000 nM SAHA-treated INTS12 KO cells compared to AAVS1 KO cells.
source: Additionally, we tested these same cells with SAHA, an HDAC inhibitor that falls within the chromatin modification LRA class, for 24 hr, and we observe greater reactivation in our 250 nM and 1000 nM SAHA-treated INTS12 KO cells compared to our AAVS1 KO cells (Figure 7B, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by RT assay data shown in Figure 7B, right panel.

claim: INTS12 knockout was able to increase reactivation with all LRAs tested.
source: Therefore, INTS12 knockout was able to increase reactivation with all LRAs tested, which supports the idea that INTS12 serves as a general block to reactivation from latency for HIV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 7B.

claim: The Integrator complex is known to regulate and attenuate transcription at promoters that are bound by pausing factors NELF and DSIF.
source: The Integrator complex is known to regulate and attenuate transcription at promoters that are bound by pausing factors NELF and DSIF (Skaar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skaar et al., 2015.

claim: HIV is known to be regulated by pausing factors NELF and DSIF.
source: HIV is known to be regulated by these pausing factors (Ping and Rana, 2001), and it has been shown that members of the Integrator are recruited to the HIV TAR loop and regulate processivity of HIV transcription (Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ping and Rana, 2001.

claim: Members of the Integrator are recruited to the HIV TAR loop and regulate processivity of HIV transcription.
source: HIV is known to be regulated by these pausing factors (Ping and Rana, 2001), and it has been shown that members of the Integrator are recruited to the HIV TAR loop and regulate processivity of HIV transcription (Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stadelmayer et al., 2014.

claim: The Integrator contains 15 members that fall within different submodules that perform various functions.
source: The Integrator contains 15 members that fall within different submodules that perform various functions (Welsh and Gardini, 2023), and of these modules some members of the cleavage, phosphatase, and core have been shown to reverse HIV latency upon knockout (Li et al., 2020; Stadelmayer et al., 2014).

claim: Some members of the cleavage, phosphatase, and core modules have been shown to reverse HIV latency upon knockout.
source: The Integrator contains 15 members that fall within different submodules that perform various functions (Welsh and Gardini, 2023), and of these modules some members of the cleavage, phosphatase, and core have been shown to reverse HIV latency upon knockout (Li et al., 2020; Stadelmayer et al., 2014).

claim: Knockout of INTS3 of the SOSS complex was not found to reverse latency in a previous study.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stadelmayer et al., 2014.

claim: Members of the core and phosphatase have been shown to improve an LRA combination of a BET inhibitor with a PKC agonist.
source: Furthermore, members of the core and phosphatase have been shown to improve an LRA combination of a BET inhibitor with a PKC agonist (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2023.

claim: The Integrator complex has been shown to modulate genes differently in the presence or absence of stress stimuli.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Tatomer et al., 2019 and Yue et al., 2017.

claim: Integrator is known to antagonize host P-TEFb function with its phosphatase module and enforce pausing at bound promoters.
source: Moreover, Integrator is known to antagonize host P-TEFb function with its phosphatase module and enforce pausing at bound promoters.

evidence: This is inferred from the known role of P-TEFb and the Integrator complex.

source: Our results are also consistent with the hypothesis that transcription elongation with INTS12 KO cells treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 may be more efficient than the LRAs alone as the levels of Ser2 phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of RNAPII are also significantly lower near the LTR, but increased distal to the LTR (Figure 5C, compare INTS12 KO treated with AZD5582 & I-BET151 to DMSO in regions 1 and 2), which may suggest RNAPII is efficiently leaving the promoter and traveling within the body of the provirus to affect full-length transcription.

source: While our data suggests that many different members of the Integrator complex could be targeted to activate HIV-1 (Figure 7A), we believe that INTS12 may be the better option to target over the rest of the complex.
evidence: This is an opinion based on the data and analysis presented.
